title: Dyspnea (Shortness of Breath) Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for dyspnea in adults, covering pulmonary, cardiac, systemic, and psychogenic etiologies. Dyspnea affects up to 25% of ambulatory patients and can be a manifestation of life-threatening disease.
source_description: Berliner D, Schneider N, Welte T, Bauersachs J. The Differential Diagnosis of Dyspnea. Dtsch Arztebl Int. 2016;113(49):834-845.

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary Embolism
key_features: Neck vein distention without lung rales

diagnoses.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
key_features: Dyspnea may be the sole presenting symptom

diagnoses.name: Pericardial Tamponade
key_features: Normal lung sounds despite hemodynamic compromise
red_flags: Beck triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds)

diagnoses.name: Congestive Heart Failure
key_features: Elevated jugular venous pressure with pulmonary rales
recommended_tests: NT-proBNP or BNP (exclusion threshold: NT-proBNP <300, BNP <100 pg/mL)

diagnoses.name: Asthma
key_features: Nocturnal symptoms and early morning worsening
red_flags: Inability to speak in full sentences

diagnoses.name: Pneumonia
key_features: Dyspnea with fever and productive cough
Dyspnea is the predominant symptom in patients over 65 (approximately 80%)

diagnoses.name: Interstitial Lung Disease
recommended_tests: Pulmonary function tests (reduced VC/TLC, decreased DLCO)

diagnoses.name: Valvular Heart Disease (Aortic Stenosis)
key_features: Exertional dyspnea with diminished exercise tolerance
Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at right upper sternal border

diagnoses.name: Anemia
key_features: Pallor of skin and mucous membranes
Tachycardia at rest or with minimal exertion
Symptoms poorly correlated with hemoglobin level

diagnoses.name: Anxiety / Panic Disorder
key_features: Dyspnea improved by distraction or exercise
Hyperventilation with perioral or extremity paresthesias
recommended_tests: ECG and basic labs to rule out organic cause

also_consider.name: Thyrotoxicosis
also_consider.rationale: Hypermetabolic state causing tachypnea and exertional dyspnea; check TSH in unexplained persistent dyspnea

also_consider.name: Neuromuscular Disease (Guillain-Barré, Myasthenia Gravis, ALS)
also_consider.rationale: Respiratory muscle weakness causing progressive dyspnea; check for proximal weakness, declining FVC

also_consider.name: Metabolic Acidosis (Kussmaul Breathing)
also_consider.rationale: Compensatory hyperventilation perceived as dyspnea; check ABG and electrolytes in diabetic or renal patients

also_consider.name: Foreign Body Aspiration
also_consider.rationale: Sudden onset in elderly or patients with impaired consciousness; unilateral wheeze or diminished breath sounds

also_consider.name: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: Dyspnea with facial and upper extremity swelling; associated with thoracic malignancy

also_consider.name: Large Pleural Effusion
also_consider.rationale: Progressive dyspnea with dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds; confirm with chest X-ray or ultrasound

also_consider.name: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: Chronic dyspnea in BMI >40 with daytime hypercapnia; elevated PaCO2 on ABG

also_consider.name: Severe Deconditioning
also_consider.rationale: Exertional dyspnea with entirely normal cardiopulmonary workup; diagnosis of exclusion

also_consider.name: Vocal Cord Dysfunction
also_consider.rationale: Inspiratory stridor mimicking asthma; poor response to bronchodilators, diagnosed by laryngoscopy during symptoms

also_consider.name: Pheochromocytoma
also_consider.rationale: Episodic dyspnea with paroxysmal hypertension, headache, and diaphoresis; check plasma metanephrines

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set, not an exhaustive differential. Consider atypical presentations, comorbidity interactions, medication effects (e.g., beta-blockers, ACE-inhibitor cough mimicking dyspnea), and diagnoses not listed here based on the specific patient's age, sex, history, and examination findings. In elderly patients, multiple simultaneous etiologies frequently coexist. In young patients with a normal workup, consider functional causes only after thorough exclusion of organic disease.
